title: I Built a Frozen-Scan Detector. A Week Later It Fires Daily — and Nothing Consumes It
author: Felixwang007
summary: This is the verdict my detector printed ten minutes ago, verbatim: $ python tools/scanfresh/scan_freshness_guard.py check \ --ledger recommendations/signal_history.jsonl \ --verify recommendations/signal_verify_log.jsonl \ --panel-dir history_ext --today 2026-10-19 verdict: FROZEN ! panel newest bar 2026-09-28 is 15 business days behind 2026-10-19 ! trailing identical run of 15 entries ( 2026-09-28 -> 2026-10-16, fp = 4c29e76725 ) ! 2 verification transition ( s ) advanced target_date without changing any measured detail Exit code 2 . Three numbers: 15 consecutive sessions whose ledger entries are identical after stripping every timestamp. 15 business days how far the data panel those sessions claim to analyse has drifted behind today. 3 — how many of those identical entries were written after I shipped this detector. The third number is the one this post is actually about. The pipeline A local Python job over a panel of per-stock daily bars: panel (3,147 JSON files, one per stock) -> classify every stock into one of six technical patterns (build_dataset_v3.compute_tech) -> append {scan_date, dist, picks} to recommendations/signal_history.jsonl -> next session, score yesterday's picks, append to signal_verify_log.jsonl It is a pure function of the panel. Which is the entire bug surface: if the panel stops being updated, the scan keeps succeeding at analysing the past. What "success" was measuring The job's contract was "append a line and exit 0". It honoured that contract 21 times in a row. Every log line green, every night at 15:35, Weekdays only. A verification ledger is supposed to answer "were yesterday's picks right?". Mine answered with the identical four per-stock returns under three different target dates, because it was re-scoring a price file whose mtime had not moved since 2026-09-28 12:10. The panel detail that makes this concrete: 3,147 files exist, but only 3,049 instruments appear on the newest bar. The other ~100 files stopped at earlier dates. Nothing complained — a file count is not a freshness measurement. Fingerprint the answer, not the activity Activity metrics — ran / exit code / rows processed / wall time — are all satisfiable by a frozen pipeline. The one reading that a frozen pipeline cannot fake is did the substance of the output change? So hash the fields that define the answer, and deliberately exclude the ones that define the run: SNAP_KEYS = ( ' dist ' , ' picks ' , ' rebound ' , ' breaks ' ) def fp ( obj , keys = SNAP_KEYS ): picked = { k : obj [ k ] for k in keys if k in obj } if not picked : # unknown shape -> whole record minus timing picked = { k : v for k , v in sorted ( obj . items ()) if k not in ( ' scan_date ' , ' verify_date ' , ' target_date ' , ' generated ' , ' run_at ' , ' ts ' )} blob = json . dumps ( picked , sort_keys = True , ensure_ascii = False ). encode () return hashlib . sha256 ( blob ). hexdigest ()[: 10 ] sort_keys=True so re-serialising a dict cannot fake a change. scan_date excluded so a date bump cannot fake one either. Anyone can recompute these fingerprints from the ledger with no access to my code. Three checks fall out of that: check reads trips when panel_stale newest bar date vs expected last trading day, in business days gap > --max-panel-gap (default 1) trailing_repeat fingerprints of consecutive ledger entries trailing identical run > --max-repeat (default 2) verify_frozen verification ledger: target_date advances while per-item detail is identical any such transition Two of the three also catch a subtler failure I had not thought about until I wrote the check: a pipeline can keep reading while its numbers stop moving, and it can keep re-dating while its measurements stay frozen. Both look like output growth. Neither is. One week later: the detector is right, and irrelevant Here is the honest part. I built this, published the tool, wrote about the failure mode — and then never wired it to the writer. Since the guard landed, the writer cron has appended three more byte-identical entries. The guard's verdict has been 2 every day. Nothing reads exit codes of a tool nothing calls. So the real lesson of this week is not "add a staleness check". It is: A detector whose verdict is not a precondition is a dashboard. A green dashboard on a frozen pipeline is worse than no dashboard, because now there are two artifacts telling you everything is fine: the writer's exit 0 and the detector's existence. The fix is one line in the writer, and I am writing it here so I have to do it: if subprocess . run ([ sys . executable , ' tools/scanfresh/scan_freshness_guard.py ' , ' check ' , ' --ledger ' , LEDGER , ' --panel-dir ' , PANEL , ' --today ' , today ]). returncode == 2 : sys . exit ( ' refusing to append a snapshot I cannot vouch for ' ) The snapshot must not be written at all. Logging the alarm while writing the stale entry anyway is the same bug with extra ceremony. Rules I now apply to any scheduled analysis job Green is not evidence. "Ran, exit 0" is a statement about the runner. Ask which reading would have been different had the job failed. If the answer is "none", you measured nothing. Ask what the job's output would look like if it were secretly frozen. That question is cheap to answer and it is where all my reliability bugs live. Fingerprint the answer, exclude the clock. Timestamps, run ids, row counts and file counts all change when nothing has changed — and none of them change when everything has. "No input" needs its own exit code. The guard returns 3 INSUFFICIENT when handed nothing to judge, because a checker that examined zero entries must never print "healthy" — the same reason a file scanner that opened zero files must never print "clean". Two identical days are normal; fifteen are not. Make the threshold explicit, tune it against your own hit rate, and remember that a single repeat is not a signal. Gate, don't report. A verdict nobody consumes is decoration. The check belongs in the writer's precondition, and the failure mode should be no snapshot written , not snapshot written plus a warning logged . The detector tools/scanfresh/scan_freshness_guard.py — stdlib only, 409 lines, exit codes 0 HEALTHY / 2 FROZEN / 3 INSUFFICIENT / 1 error, with an 18-assertion selftest over synthetic fixtures: python tools/scanfresh/scan_freshness_guard.py selftest # 18/18 passed python tools/scanfresh/scan_freshness_guard.py check \ --ledger samples/real_frozen_history.jsonl \ --verify samples/real_verify_frozen.jsonl \ --today 2026-10-12 # exit 2, FROZEN samples/ ships the real frozen ledgers (the 16-entry one with the trailing run of 10, and its verification ledger), so the FROZEN verdict is reproducible on your machine without my data, plus a synthetic healthy ledger so the pass path is testable too. Code, samples, notes: https://github.com/Felixwang007/awesome-content-tools/tree/main/tools/scanfresh — MIT, take the 400 lines and skip the essay. One caveat I would rather state than have you discover: this detects frozen output , not a broken fetch . A source that returns different garbage every day passes all three checks. Freshness is necessary, not sufficient. The obvious next gap in mine is a China exchange holiday calendar — right now panel_stale knows weekends but treats October's exchange holidays as ordinary business days, which is exactly how a 15-day gap reads as ordinary Monday drift. If you build analysis agents you actually run daily — screening, scheduled scans, anything that appends a snapshot and exits 0 — the same guard is packaged as a skill on 虾评 ( xiaping.coze.com ) next to the A-share three-pillar screener, and the raw script is in the repo above. All numbers here are from a single check run against the real ledger and panel on 2026-10-19; the ledger, verification log and panel are a private workspace, but the guard and the exact frozen ledgers it trips on are public in samples/ .

title: RepoTrace — Make failing commands repeatable, inspectable, and testable
author: Biki Kc
summary: Why it matters When a command fails in your project or CI, “it failed” is rarely enough to act on. RepoTrace saves the exact argv, exit code, stdout/stderr, working directory, and interpreter metadata so a failure becomes a replayable artifact — a single-file, JSON bug report that you can rerun, render as Markdown, or convert into a standalone pytest regression test. That preserves the signal of the original failure and turns debugging into a repeatable, auditable process. What RepoTrace is RepoTrace is a small Python CLI and library (Python 3.12+) that captures command runs and produces: Structured bug reports persisted as JSON files under a report store (.repotrace/reports by default). Replay functionality to re-run recorded commands and compare results to the original trace. Markdown rendering for human-friendly reports. Generation of self-contained pytest regression tests that embed the command and expected output. Core benefits Reproducibility: replay a failure later (or on another machine) to confirm whether it still reproduces. Traceability: keep a single-file record suitable for committing alongside a codebase or attaching to an issue. CI friendliness: use capture/replay in pipelines to collect failing commands automatically and assert regressions as tests. Fast triage: readable Markdown and tests remove context-switching and guesswork from debugging. Quick highlights Language: Python 3.12+ CLI: repotrace (Typer-based) Notable libraries: Pydantic v2 (structured models), Rich (console output), Typer (CLI) License: MIT Why teams should try RepoTrace Speed up debugging: capturing everything about a failing command means no more “works on my machine” guessing. Create durable artifacts: JSON reports are easy to inspect, diff, and commit; generated tests are ready to land in CI. Reduce friction between triage and fix: a report plus a generated test gives a precise spec of the problem that a reviewer or teammate can reproduce **locally. Installation & Resources ReproTrace is distributed under the MIT license and can be installed using standard Python package managers: PyPI: https://pypi.org/project/repotrace/ GitHub Repository: https://github.com/BiTech5/repotrace Join the Journey Join RepoTrace — short invite RepoTrace turns failing commands into replayable bug reports and ready-to-commit regression tests — help make debugging reproducible. Quick start Fork & clone https://github.com/BiTech5/repotrace uv sync && source .venv/bin/activate Run a focused test: .venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/test_replay.py -q Good first contributions Fix small bugs, improve README examples, add edge-case tests, or generate CI/usage walkthroughs. Conclusion / Call to action RepoTrace reduces the time and friction of turning an observed failure into a replayable, testable artifact. If your team spends time reproducing flaky or intermittent failures, trying RepoTrace on a representative failing command (or a CI job) can immediately pay dividends: you get a concrete, versionable report and the option to convert it into a regression test that prevents regressions from returning. title: Every DOE 202(c) emergency order of 2025-2026 in one CSV: 66 this year, and emergency orders in force on 76 days
author: munimv2
summary: The U.S. Department of Energy can order a utility or grid operator to keep running generation under section 202(c) of the Federal Power Act. DOE lists those orders on its website as text. I put every order, extension and amendment from DOE's 2025 and 2026 pages into one CSV (85 rows), with a small standard-library Python script whose tests check the counts against the table. title: I built a workflow that checks whether my AI agent's context was enough, then proves it with my own tests
author: Ryan Cotten
summary: When I give an AI coding agent a task, I never actually know if the context I sent it was enough. So I built the check. The stack is four small tools, all Python standard library, all MIT, all local: GhostSlice cuts a project down to a task bundle and reports the token cut. On my own bench repo: 74,692 tokens full, 29,926 sliced. GhostVerify checks the bundle against the task before an agent runs, and says gaps_found when something reachable is missing. GhostBench runs the same task full vs sliced and, when you give it a test command, executes your tests in a contained runner (scrubbed environment, your secrets never reach the test process) and labels the result honestly: static analysis is not called a live run. GhostConsole renders one board from all of it, and its Verified column now names the strongest evidence behind it and counts the checks that are missing. A fifth tool, ghostworkflow, runs the chain in one command, and a small local web app puts a face on it. I ran the whole thing on its own repo and published the result warts and all: verdict attention, 2 verify gaps, and a test failure that turned out to be a path assumption in one of my own tests. The first dogfood run also caught a real bug in the contained runner (it hid the user site-packages, so pytest vanished), which is fixed and shipped. I am looking for 5 to 10 developers who use AI coding agents daily to run it on one of their own repos and tell me where it breaks or bores them. Quickstart is 6 clones and one command. title: Hybrid Search for RAG: Why Your Vector Search Misses "TS-999" (and the 20-Line Fix)
author: M.T.Ramkrushna
summary: A user types: "How do I fix error TS-999?" Your RAG app runs a vector search, pulls five chunks about error codes in general , and the model writes a confident, useless answer. The one doc that literally says "TS-999" never made it into the prompt. That is not a model problem. It is a retrieval problem, and it has a boring, reliable fix: hybrid search . Why pure vector search misses exact matches Embeddings are great at meaning. "Reset my password" and "I can't log in" land close together, which is exactly what you want. But embeddings compress text into a point in space. Rare, exact tokens get blurred in that compression: Error codes and ticket IDs ( TS-999 , INC-4821 ) SKUs, part numbers, invoice numbers Function and config names ( max_retries , PG_POOL_SIZE ) Names of people, products, and internal tools To an embedding model, TS-999 and TS-998 look almost identical. To your user, they are completely different problems. Anthropic's Contextual Retrieval write-up uses this exact example: an embedding model "might find content about error codes in general, but could miss the exact 'TS-999' match." Keyword search finds it instantly. The fix: run both searches, then fuse the rankings Hybrid search means you run two retrievers on every query: BM25 (keyword search). Scores chunks by exact term matches, weighted by how rare the term is. It is the classic search-engine ranking function and it loves IDs and jargon. Vector search (semantic). Scores chunks by meaning. It handles paraphrases, synonyms, and vague questions. Then you merge the two ranked lists. The simplest merge that works well is Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) : score(chunk) = Σ 1 / (k + rank_in_list) You add up the score from each list the chunk appears in. k is a constant, usually 60 , from the original RRF paper by Cormack, Clarke and Büttcher (SIGIR 2009) . Elasticsearch uses the same default for its rank_constant in its RRF docs . The nice part: RRF only looks at ranks , not raw scores. You never have to figure out how a BM25 score of 14.2 compares to a cosine similarity of 0.81. A minimal Python version This uses rank_bm25 for keyword search and whatever vector search you already have. from rank_bm25 import BM25Okapi chunks = load_chunks () # list[str] bm25 = BM25Okapi ([ c . lower (). split () for c in chunks ]) def keyword_search ( query : str , n : int = 50 ) -> list [ int ]: scores = bm25 . get_scores ( query . lower (). split ()) return sorted ( range ( len ( chunks )), key = lambda i : scores [ i ], reverse = True )[: n ] def vector_search ( query : str , n : int = 50 ) -> list [ int ]: ... # your existing embedding search, returning chunk indices in rank order def rrf ( * ranked_lists : list [ int ], k : int = 60 ) -> list [ int ]: fused : dict [ int , float ] = {} for ranked in ranked_lists : for rank , idx in enumerate ( ranked , start = 1 ): fused [ idx ] = fused . get ( idx , 0.0 ) + 1.0 / ( k + rank ) return sorted ( fused , key = fused . get , reverse = True ) def hybrid_search ( query : str , top_k : int = 10 ) -> list [ str ]: ids = rrf ( keyword_search ( query ), vector_search ( query )) return [ chunks [ i ] for i in ids [: top_k ]] In production you usually don't hand-roll BM25. Postgres full-text search, Elasticsearch/OpenSearch, and vector databases like Weaviate ship hybrid search built in. The logic is the same. How much does it help? In Anthropic's experiments across codebases, fiction, and papers, combining embeddings with BM25 beat embeddings alone, and adding context to chunks plus BM25 cut top-20 retrieval failures by 49% (5.7% to 2.9%). Adding a reranker on top cut failures by 67% (5.7% to 1.9%). Source: Introducing Contextual Retrieval . Your numbers will differ. That's why the next section matters. A practical rollout plan Collect 30–50 real queries from logs, and make sure some contain IDs, codes, or exact names. Label the right chunk for each query. Measure recall@10 for vector-only search. That's your baseline. Add BM25 + RRF and measure again. Look especially at the ID-heavy queries. Optionally add a reranker (retrieve ~50–150, rerank, keep the top 10–20). Keep the eval set in the repo so the next "small retrieval tweak" can't silently undo it. When you can skip it Your queries are all fuzzy, natural-language questions with no IDs or jargon. Your knowledge base is small enough to just put in the prompt (Anthropic suggests under ~200k tokens is worth trying first). Everyone else: if your users ever type a code, a name, or a number, give them keyword search back. TL;DR Vector search is great at meaning and bad at exact tokens. BM25 is great at exact tokens and bad at meaning. Run both, merge with Reciprocal Rank Fusion (k = 60), and measure recall on real queries. References Anthropic, Introducing Contextual Retrieval (Sep 2024) Cormack, Clarke, Büttcher, Reciprocal Rank Fusion outperforms Condorcet and individual Rank Learning Methods (SIGIR 2009) Elastic, Reciprocal rank fusion docs Weaviate, Hybrid search docs rank_bm25 on GitHub What's in your retrieval stack today: vector-only, or hybrid?

title: PSEC-99: A 3D Browser Game in C# and WASM, Without WebGL
author: Umberto Giacobbi
summary: Take a look at what the OpenSilver team has built. This game shows what C# and WebAssembly can do in the browser. How fast? Play it and see for yourself. Disclosure: I used to work with this team, so I know what they’re capable of. For those who don't know, OpenSilver was born long ago as a replacement for Silverlight, a kind of competitor to Flash (but way better). But, as usual, Microsoft killed it. Classic: from "this is the future" to "nah, HTML5 and React are the future." It compiles high-level code into pure WebAssembly, which is fast, really fast. It can do a lot more nowadays (it supports WPF, third-party controls, MAUI, full C#/WebAssembly interop and more). To be honest, a demo like this also raises an awkward question: why do so many web apps struggle with CPU and memory usage just to display a few hundred divs? One day I will have an answer to this. So, what did they do? They took a 1982 TI-99/4A game and turned it into a 3D browser experience using C#/WASM and an int[] pixel buffer. No WebGL. In other words, they write the pixels directly, without a middleman. Everything is done through their code. I repeat their buffer is one pixel! The result is PSEC-99 , an unofficial 3D tribute to PARSEC . Try it yourself Both the game and OpenSilver are open source, so you can study the code, extend it or just play. What caught my attention is the rendering approach. Their entire 3D scene is drawn in C# into a single pixel buffer (yes, just one!) in .NET memory, then displayed on an HTML canvas through OpenSilver 3.4 Preview’s new WriteableImage XAML control. That means no game engine, WebGL or WebGPU renderer: the 3D math, projection and rasterization happen in C#. Terrain, stars, buildings, enemies, lasers and explosions all end up in that array. They kept other parts deliberately old-school too: The terrain is rendered row by row, filling pixels directly rather than drawing terrain polygons. Buildings start as ASCII grids in C#. Sounds and voices are synthesized at runtime. If you remember PARSEC on the TI-99/4A, give it a try. And if you’re into .NET, retro computing or software rendering, the source is well worth exploring. Explore the MIT-licensed source code — open it in the .NET IDE to run, edit, fork or download it. Play directly in your browser — it runs on .NET 10/WASM, including on phones. Heads up: it has sound!

title: A Practice Planner Should Advance on a Verdict, Not a Stopwatch
author: Giang Pham Truong
summary: Disclosure: I’m Giang Pham, Pianory’s maker. AI helped draft this article and review its claims against the repository. It describes source behavior and existing unit-test cases, not a runtime study or evidence of better learning outcomes. A practice app can measure how long a screen stayed open. That does not tell it whether a pianist can play the passage. If a planner treats time or a fast playback setting as proof of progress, it can make a difficult task harder for the wrong reason. Pianory’s goal planner uses a smaller, visible signal: the learner’s own verdict after a task. Its session form offers “Still stuck,” “Playable slowly,” and “Fairly steady.” The session record separately stores the player tempo, and the type comment explicitly says that percentage is “not a measure of skill.” The planner does not listen to the piano or verify the learner’s assessment. Make the next step a rule someone can inspect The planner filters to sessions for one goal and ignores review sessions, then reads the newest ordinary session. Its basic ladder is straightforward: “Still stuck” lowers the same hand setup by 10 percentage points. “Playable slowly,” or no rating, repeats the same hand setup and tempo. “Fairly steady” moves a two-hand goal from one hand to the other, then to both hands once the other hand was also steady at that tempo. After both hands are steady, the tempo rises in 10-point steps up to the goal’s target. That target is at least the written tempo and can be higher if the learner chose a higher goal tempo. At the target, the planner suggests completion and a whole-passage task. Here is the core boundary in the implementation: const tempo = last . playbackTempoPercent ; if ( last . rating === ' stuck ' ) { tasks . push ( task ( ' slower ' , passage , last . hands , tempo - TEMPO_STEP )); } else if ( last . rating !== ' steady ' ) { tasks . push ( task ( ' repeat ' , passage , last . hands , tempo )); } TEMPO_STEP is 10. The separate steady branch chooses the next hand, both hands, or the next tempo step. The planner returns advice; it does not turn every elapsed minute into a promotion. Check the boundary with awkward inputs Suppose a goal covers bars 9–16 for both hands at 60% of the written tempo. The first plan asks for the right and left hands separately at 60%. After a steady right-hand session, it asks for the left hand. Once each hand has been steady at 60%, it asks for both hands at 60%. After a steady both-hands session, it can ask for 70%. If the learner instead reports being stuck at 90%, the next task is the same hand setup at 80%. The repository’s unit-test examples also probe misleading signals. One gives a session 86,400 practiced seconds and a 140% playback tempo but rates it “Playable slowly”; the expected task is still a repeat at 140%, not a harder step. Another checks that a steady session at 95% advances to 100%, rather than skipping past the target. These are source tests I inspected; I did not run them for this draft. That suggests a useful test pattern for any adaptive workflow: hold the learner’s explicit verdict constant while making the tempting proxy extreme. A long session with a “stuck” verdict should not advance. A short session rated steady should follow the rule’s next step. The assertion should check the returned task, not just that a planner function ran. Keep the limits visible A self-rating is still a self-rating. Pianory’s code can use it to suggest a smaller next task, but it cannot establish accuracy, comfortable fingering, or whether a learner played the passage correctly. That is a deliberate product boundary in this implementation, and it keeps the planner’s promise modest: help choose what to work on next from information the learner actually supplied. The useful engineering idea is not that every practice app needs this exact ladder. It is that a recommendation should name the signal that moves it forward, keep unrelated telemetry out of that decision, and make the rule easy to test. What input should count as evidence of progress in a learning product?

title: Google found my side page before my main feature
author: TattooTryOn
summary: I launched TattooTryOn a few days ago. You upload a photo of your arm or leg, drop a design on it, place it yourself, and an AI model turns the flat artwork into something that looks like actual ink in skin. That's the product. That's the thing I spent most of my time on. Google doesn't care. This morning (Oct 19), Search Console showed the site's first impressions. Two queries: "tattoo design font generator" and "tattoo text font generator". Average position 24.8, so page three, nobody clicking. Still, it's the first signal I've had from search, and it points at the tattoo font generator , a side page I built almost as an afterthought. Nothing about the try-on. I find this a little funny and a little annoying. The numbers so far Plausible says that through Oct 18 the site had 13 unique visitors and 100 pageviews. Tiny. But the average visit was close to 11 minutes, which I didn't expect for a tool you could, in theory, use in one go. Where they came from: 7 direct, 6 from V2EX, 1 from Google. One V2EX post brought in about 40% of the visits. Visitors came from the US, China, Japan, and Thailand, which is a wider spread than 13 people should honestly produce. I'm not going to pretend these numbers mean much. They don't. But writing them down is useful, because in a month I'll want to know where I started. Why the font page might be the easier one to rank Thinking about it for more than five minutes, it makes sense. A query like "tattoo text font generator" describes exactly what the page does. Type some text, see it in a bunch of fonts, download a transparent PNG. The search intent and the page line up one-to-one. There's no explaining needed. "AI tattoo try-on" is a newer kind of thing. People search for it, but they phrase it a dozen different ways ("see tattoo on my arm", "tattoo preview app", "how would a tattoo look on me"), and the page has to convince you before it's useful. That's harder for a brand-new domain to win. Also, the font page is just text and fonts. No model, no credits, no waiting. It works the instant it loads, which probably doesn't hurt. Why it has no AI in it This is the part I actually care about from a dev point of view. Lettering is where image models are weakest. Ask one to render a name and you'll get letters that look plausible and are sometimes wrong. For a tattoo, one wrong letter is the whole problem. So the font generator just renders real font files on a canvas. A font file doesn't hallucinate. The try-on side is built around the same idea of not letting the model decide things it shouldn't. Placement happens in the browser by hand, before any model runs. The editor keeps a center point (normalized to the photo, so it survives resizing), a scale, and an angle. Before calling the renderer, those get baked into pixels. The model gets two pixel-aligned images: the original photo, and a composite with the design drawn onto it. // simplified function bake ( photo , design , { cx , cy , scale , angle }) { const c = new OffscreenCanvas ( photo . width , photo . height ); const ctx = c . getContext ( ' 2d ' ); ctx . drawImage ( photo , 0 , 0 ); ctx . translate ( cx * photo . width , cy * photo . height ); ctx . rotate ( angle ); ctx . scale ( scale , scale ); ctx . globalCompositeOperation = ' multiply ' ; ctx . drawImage ( design , - design . width / 2 , - design . height / 2 ); return c ; } The composite uses multiply blending, so ink can only darken skin, never lighten it. Skin texture shows through, and the preview you see in the editor looks the same as what gets sent to the model. There's also a body segmentation step that cuts the design out wherever it lands on clothes, hair or jewelry, so the model doesn't paint a tattoo onto your sleeve. Placement is free, too. You can move things around as long as you want and nothing is generated until you press the button. Maybe that's where some of those 11 minutes go. I don't know yet. What I'm doing with this Not much, honestly, other than paying attention. I'm not going to rebuild the homepage around fonts because of two queries at position 24.8. But it's a reminder that the simple, boring, clearly named page is often the one search engines understand first, and I should probably write landing pages for the try-on that describe it in plain words people actually type. And I should post on V2EX again, apparently. If you've launched something where the side tool got noticed before the main product, I'm curious whether you leaned into it or ignored it.

title: SellCraft AI: a listing writer that runs on the seller's laptop, not my server
author: Senthil raja .R
summary: (alt: SellCraft AI — a fully local Etsy/eBay listing writer with Gemma 4 and Ollama) This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle What I Built SellCraft AI is a listing writer that runs on the seller's laptop, not on anyone else's server. A handmade seller drops in up to four product photos, types the few facts only the maker knows — materials, size, price — picks a platform (Etsy or eBay) and a tone, and gets back a finished listing: a keyword-front-loaded title inside the platform's character limit, a 120–180 word description in the shop's own voice, and tags that respect Etsy's 13-tags-by-20-characters rule. I built it for one specific person — the seller I kept picturing while writing it: forty active listings, a day job, a phone full of product photos. Photographing six new mugs takes an evening. Writing the six listings takes another evening , and that's the evening the box stays closed and the mugs stay unlisted. SellCraft turns each listing into about a minute of work — and it doesn't sound like a template, because it writes from the photos and the seller's own words instead of from a blank prompt box. Would someone pay for it? I think so, and not much has to be true for that to hold: it saves a seller an evening a week, and it's sold as a flat one-time download. There's no API bill behind it, so there's no meter to hide inside a subscription — the seller can regenerate a description twenty times without watching a counter. Tooling for a side hustle shouldn't be one of the side hustle's fixed costs, and only a locally-running model makes that price possible. Demo There's no live link, deliberately. SellCraft's whole argument is that it runs on the seller's machine — a hosted demo would be a different, worse product. The honest demo is two commands: ollama pull gemma4 # one-time: the model now lives on this machine python sellcraft.py # opens http://127.0.0.1:8765 The repo ships three sample photos (a mug, soap bars, earrings), so you can go from clone to a finished listing in about a minute without hunting for product photos. Code Everything lives in one repo: https://github.com/Senthil455/Sell-Carft-AI One Python file (~600 lines, standard library only), one plain HTML/CSS/JS front end, one SQLite file. No pip install, no build step, no framework, no account. Built end-to-end for this challenge. How I Built It A single-file backend, on purpose. The server is http.server + urllib + sqlite3 — every import is in Python's standard library. If you're going to ask a stranger to run AI on their own laptop, "you can read the entire backend in one sitting" is the feature. The trust story is the source code, not a policy page. Gemma reads the photos. The app talks to Ollama on 127.0.0.1:11434 and runs Gemma's vision model. Seeing the photo is what makes or breaks the output: it has to recognize speckled stoneware with a chunky handle, because "handmade ceramic mug" is the listing every other seller already has. Any vision model you've pulled shows up in a dropdown, so a slower laptop can swap down. The prompt is where the product actually lives. It's one carefully-built template with hard rules: never invent materials, sizes, prices or origins; work only from the seller's facts and what's clearly visible in the photos; plain text only; exactly four labelled sections (NOTES / TITLE / DESCRIPTION / TAGS). Each platform carries its own constraints — Etsy gets a 100–140 character title and 13 tags of ≤20 characters; eBay gets a keyword-first 80-character title and 8 keywords. My favourite part is NOTES: instead of inventing a size, the model says what it saw and asks about the one thing it couldn't read — "roughly how much does this hold?" A writer that asks is worth more than one that guesses. Trust is enforced a second time, in code. Prompts drift, so every draft passes through a tidy_listing() cleanup before it reaches the UI: titles are truncated at a word boundary to the platform's limit, tags are deduplicated, lowercased and trimmed to 20 characters — and when trimming would gut a tag into nonsense, it's dropped instead of shipped broken. (Etsy silently ignores over-long tags, which is how sellers end up with nine working tags and no idea why.) Streaming, because good writing feels written. The server relays Ollama's token stream to the browser, so you watch the title fill in, character counters tick against each platform's limits, and tags that run long light up red before Etsy ever sees them. A full draft lands in about [X] seconds at [Y] tok/s on my laptop — the app prints both numbers under every draft, so the machine is honest about its speed with the seller. It learns the shop's voice, locally. Saved listings go into SQLite, and the last three are fed back into the next prompt as a style sample: match this voice, never copy it. The output sounds more like the shop with every listing — and the examples never leave the machine that wrote them. Revision works the same way: type "less flowery" or "make the description shorter", and the model receives the previous draft plus the instruction, and rewrites the whole thing. Small kindnesses where they matter. Photos are downscaled in the browser to 1000 px before they hit the local model. The app opens its own tab on startup. When Ollama isn't running, the page says so in plain words and offers a re-check button instead of dying. And there's a one-click CSV export, because a seller's catalogue is their business, not my database. What it deliberately doesn't do: it won't post to Etsy for you. The output is plain text with copy buttons, because holding a seller's marketplace credentials is a commitment a v1 shouldn't make. It's probably the first thing a real user will ask for — and that's a decision to make with a real user, not on their behalf. Why Does Open Innovation Matter? Privacy is the architecture, not a promise. The only hostname that appears anywhere in SellCraft's source is 127.0.0.1 . A handmade seller's photos are their original work — often photographed before the listing exists anywhere — and their drafts contain pricing and positioning they haven't published yet. Running Gemma locally means there is no server to trust. That's a different category of claim from "we don't store your data": you can verify it by reading one file. The business model only works because inference is local. With a closed API, every draft is a line item, and the builder pays for every user forever. That cost structure is exactly what pushes small tools into subscriptions, credit packs, and "fair use" limits. Gemma on the laptop makes the hundredth listing cost the same as the first — nothing — so the product can be sold as a flat one-time download. A price that works for a seller in a craft economy only exists because the marginal cost is zero. Swapping models is a feature, not an escape hatch. The model dropdown is just "whatever you've pulled with Ollama." When a better open-weight vision model ships next month, a seller gets it with one command: no waitlist, no repricing, no migration project. Whole product roadmaps have been broken by a provider deprecating a single endpoint. The agent's behaviour is a text file. "Never invent a size" is a visible rule in one f-string that a seller — or anyone forking the repo — can change in a line. Closed systems hand you a prompt box; open ones hand you the harness. And because Gemma's weights are open, the natural next step stays on the table instead of on a waitlist: fine-tuning a small model on a shop's own back catalogue, so the writer learns their catalogue the way a hired copywriter would. It works with the Wi-Fi off. Once the model is pulled, SellCraft doesn't need the internet to write a listing — on a train, at a market stall, during an outage. That still feels slightly magic, and it's the property that most cleanly separates what open weights make possible from what closed APIs allow. My Agent Session My First User Prize Categories Best Use of Gemma. Gemma is the core of the product, running locally through Ollama: it reads the seller's photos and writes every word of the listing — the description, the title, the tags, and the questions it asks back. The default pull is gemma4:latest ; any Gemma vision build works, and there is no other model or cloud API anywhere in the stack.

title: OpenRouter's Armor Vets Agent Tool Calls. In Claude Code Mode It Only Flags Them
author: Gabriel Anhaia
summary: Book: System Design Pocket Guide: Fundamentals Also by me: Thinking in Go (2-book series) — Complete Guide to Go Programming + Hexagonal Architecture in Go My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub Your agent decides to delete a folder you never mentioned. Somewhere between the model and your shell, something has to say no. On October 15, OpenRouter launched Armor in beta to be that something. Armor is a safety classifier that sits between the model and your application and checks every tool call against rules you write in plain English. A flagged call isn't executed, and the model is told which rule it hit. GIGAZINE covered the launch on October 16. There is one mode where "isn't executed" depends on you. On the Messages API, in the mode built for Claude Code, Armor keeps the flagged tool_use in the response and only marks it. The docs say it plainly: "Under claude_code_compatibility your application is what stops the call." In the flow the docs describe, Claude Code is that application: it reads the flagged verdict, declines the call and writes an is_error tool result. The gap is a Messages client of your own that never reads the verdict. What Armor checks, and with what For each tool call, OpenRouter sends the call, your rules and the conversation to a decision model, which returns a probability that the call matches each rule ( Armor docs ). Armor folds those into one verdict: flagged or not_flagged . OpenRouter's launch post names the model: TypeSafe's Jev. Jev is a structured decision model that returns typed answers with probabilities instead of generated text, and that guide lists typesafe/jev-1.14 as the current release. Why a model and not a pattern list? OpenRouter's pitch is that "regex-based filtering often isn't enough to detect unwanted tool calls" ( launch post ). The launch post also says Armor beats Claude Code's own auto-mode classifier on performance and cost. A review on explainx.ai points out that OpenRouter hasn't published a test set or numbers behind that claim. I haven't run Armor myself. Three kinds of rules Rules come in three tiers ( Armor docs ): hard_deny is "for actions that must never happen, regardless of what the user says." soft_deny is "for actions that are usually wrong but are sometimes requested legitimately." A match blocks the call unless an allow rule also matches or the user asked for that exact operation on that exact target in the conversation. allow "never blocks anything. It defines exceptions to soft-deny rules." Armor also has a built-in soft-deny for limits the user set in the conversation and hasn't lifted, such as "don't push until I review" ( docs ). Each rule takes an id , an optional name , instructions and an optional threshold . The defaults are 0.6 for deny rules and 0.7 for allow rules. Here's a Responses API request with one rule in each deny tier, in audit mode. The shape follows the docs' example request ; the rules and the environment entry are mine. Save it as request.json : { "model" : "openai/gpt-4.1" , "input" : "Clear out the build cache." , "tools" : [{ "type" : "function" , "name" : "bash" , "description" : "Run a shell command" , "parameters" : { "type" : "object" , "properties" : { "command" : { "type" : "string" } }, "required" : [ "command" ] } }], "plugins" : [{ "id" : "armor" , "mode" : "audit" , "output_mode" : "custom_item" , "classifier_context" : { "v" : 1 , "auto_mode" : { "environment" : [ { "name" : "deploy_target" , "value" : "staging" } ], "hard_deny" : [{ "id" : "no-secret-egress" , "instructions" : "Never upload .env files or API keys." }], "soft_deny" : [{ "id" : "no-deletes" , "instructions" : "Do not delete files outside ./build." }] } } }] } Then send it: curl https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/responses \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $OPENROUTER_API_KEY " \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d @request.json With "mode": "audit" , Armor scores every call and blocks nothing, so you can tune rules against real traffic before you enforce them ( docs ). Remove that line to enforce. Audit mode can't be combined with claude_code_compatibility . Where a blocked call ends up What a block looks like depends on output_mode ( Armor docs ): output_mode API A blocked call shows up as text (default on Chat Completions and Responses) Chat Completions, Responses An <openrouter_armor_blocked> marker in the assistant text custom_item Responses An openrouter:armor_blocked output item claude_code_compatibility Messages The tool_use , kept, marked flagged in safeguard_results In the first two modes a blocked call never reaches your code. The model is told the call "was blocked by OpenRouter Armor by the rule" it matched, "and was not executed." It's also told: "Do not retry it with the same arguments." ( docs ) The third mode works differently. A Messages request that carries a safeguards entry of type dangerous_tool_use selects it on its own, with no plugins entry ( docs ). Then the docs warn: "A Messages client that ignores safeguard_results will run a flagged tool_use ." If your client might not check, the docs suggest "output_mode": "text" instead. If you write your own Messages client against this, check before you execute. Per the docs , safeguard_results is a top-level array, and each entry's status.tool_uses is keyed by tool call id, with a type , an outcome and an optional explanation . This TypeScript helper runs a call only when Armor evaluated it and didn't flag it: type Verdict = { type : string ; outcome ?: " flagged " | " not_flagged " ; explanation ?: string ; }; // Run a tool_use only if Armor evaluated it and let it // through. A missing or unavailable verdict is a refusal. function mayRun ( response : any , toolUseId : string ): boolean { for ( const r of response . safeguard_results ?? []) { const v : Verdict | undefined = r . status ?. tool_uses ?.[ toolUseId ]; if ( v ) { return v . type === " evaluated " && v . outcome === " not_flagged " ; } } return false ; } Refusing missing and unavailable verdicts is my choice, not something the docs require. It mirrors the on_error default Armor uses for plugin requests, which is next. Fail closed or fail open The decision model can time out, error out or get a request too large to judge. The verdict is then unavailable , and on_error decides what happens: block , the default, or log ( Armor docs ). That setting doesn't reach the Claude Code mode. There, per the docs, "an unavailable call is always released with its verdict visible," so your client decides. A few more edges, all from the docs : Armor isn't supported yet for requests under HIPAA, Zero Data Retention or a data-region restriction. Plugin requests there are rejected with a 403. Claude Code requests are released with an unavailable verdict instead, and Claude Code falls back to its own local auto-mode check. Under Zero Data Retention, Armor isn't the one screening those calls today. The decision model can produce false positives and misses. Per-rule threshold is the knob for that. With the Claude Code-compatible rule set loaded, Armor "added 279 ms of latency at the median and 334 ms at the 90th percentile." "During the beta, evaluation is not billed." OpenRouter says pricing comes before general availability, and that configuration fields, the safeguard_results object and the openrouter:armor_blocked item type may still change. That third bullet is a per-tool-call cost. An agent turn that fires several tool calls can pay it on each one. Running Claude Code through it Armor's Claude Code path goes through Ori , OpenRouter's launcher that runs an agent CLI you already have on OpenRouter. It signs you in with OAuth instead of a pasted key, and it lists Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Cline and others. The Ori guide installs it with a script; read it before you pipe it into a shell: curl -fsSL https://openrouter.ai/labs/ori/install.sh | bash The Armor docs then start Claude Code on a non-Anthropic model with auto mode on, and say no plugins entry is needed: ori claude --model moonshotai/kimi-k2-0905 -- --permission-mode auto In Claude Code's auto mode , "a second model, the classifier, reviews actions instead of you." GIGAZINE reports that through Ori, models on OpenRouter can use that approval mechanism with Armor doing the review. I build Hermes IDE, so weigh this paragraph with that in mind. Hermes runs every agent in a real terminal and takes any command-line agent you add, so the ori claude line above can go in as a Custom agent next to Claude Code and Codex, with each task on its own branch and worktree. Hermes never answers a permission prompt for you, and it doesn't read Armor's verdicts: that check happens between Claude Code and OpenRouter. I haven't run Ori through Hermes myself. The ⌘N agent picker in Hermes 2.3.4: Claude Code and Codex installed, the other supported agents listed, and Custom agent for any other command. Before you turn it on If you're trying Armor this week, settle three things first: Start in "mode": "audit" and read the verdicts on your own traffic before you let anything block. On Chat Completions and Responses, pick on_error on purpose. block keeps a dead checker from waving calls through; log keeps a dead checker from stopping your agent. If you own a Messages client, check safeguard_results before every tool_use , or use "output_mode": "text" . Would you put a second model in front of every tool call your agent makes, at roughly 300 ms each? Or do you trust a permission prompt and your own eyes more? Tell me in the comments. If this was useful I build Hermes IDE , a free, source-available console for running Claude Code, Codex and other agents side by side, on macOS, Windows and Linux. Armor puts a network hop and a fail-open-or-fail-closed decision in front of every action your agent takes. Latency budgets, timeouts and what a system does when a dependency stops answering are the core of the System Design Pocket Guide: Fundamentals , and they apply to an agent's safety check as much as to a payment service.

title: Choosing an AI Resource Management Tool: A Decision Guide for 2026
author: Sara Ebden
summary: When several teams are overbooked while a specialist has spare capacity, managers need more than a staffing calendar. Useful resource planning connects demand and availability to assignments, actual effort, project status, and portfolio priorities. This guide compares six tools across portfolio visibility, resource scheduling, worklog evidence, delivery reporting, workflow fit, and AI actionability. The right choice depends on whether your priority is connected portfolio decisions, professional-services utilization, flexible work management, or straightforward scheduling. Comparison table Tool Best For Deployment AI Agent Readiness Pricing Key Feature Free Plan ONES.com Portfolio and resource decisions connected to delivery work Cloud, On-Premise, Private Cloud, Air-gapped Yes, AI agent + MCP Free up to 30 seats; tiered pricing. Connects requirements, projects, tasks, risks, time logs, resource scheduling, worklog reporting, delivery metrics, and dashboards Yes — up to 30 seats Monday Flexible resource coordination across departments Cloud Native agent Contact sales Customizable boards, workload views, and automations Yes Wrike Enterprise work management with workload visibility Cloud Native agent Contact sales Workload planning, project tracking, and cross-team reporting Yes Kantata Professional services utilization and forecasting Cloud AI assistant Contact sales Resource forecasting, utilization management, and project financial context No Mosaic Capacity planning for services and delivery teams Cloud AI assistant Contact sales Capacity planning, allocations, utilization, and forecasting No Float Simple team scheduling and capacity planning Cloud Not yet Contact sales Visual schedules, allocations, time tracking, and availability planning Yes Evaluation criteria A resource calendar is only one part of the decision. Evaluate whether the tool can connect staffing choices to current delivery work: Portfolio visibility: Can you relate strategic requirements and active projects to risks, delivery status, and competing priorities? Capacity and scheduling: Can managers compare availability, planned work, assignments, and demand before committing people? Time and worklog evidence: Can recorded effort inform estimates, utilization reviews, and future allocations? Delivery reporting: Do dashboards and metrics show how staffing decisions affect progress, risks, and outcomes? Workflow fit: Can resource decisions stay connected to the tasks, projects, approvals, and updates where teams work? AI actionability: Can AI or connected agents use authorized project context to analyze work or update workflows, rather than creating a separate planning silo? For example, a portfolio lead should be able to spot an overloaded team, review affected risks and milestones, compare available capacity, and decide whether to change assignments. Shortlist ONES.com: Best for connecting portfolio priorities, resource capacity, project risks, time logs, and delivery dashboards. Its AI works with shared project context, and MCP can connect authorized external agents. Monday: Best for flexible boards and workload views that adapt to different departments. Wrike: Best for larger organizations combining workload planning with structured project reporting. Kantata: Best for professional-services utilization, forecasting, and project financial context. Mosaic: Best for capacity planning, allocations, and forward-looking resource decisions. Float: Best for a clear schedule of availability, assignments, and planned time. Detailed reviews ONES.com Product Overview ONES.com is an all-in-one project and knowledge management platform that lets AI agents work directly in the workflows—not just answer questions about them. For AI resource management, it connects requirements, projects, tasks, risks, time logs, resource schedules, delivery metrics, and dashboards so portfolio and team decisions use shared work data instead of disconnected spreadsheets. ONES Assistant can analyze project progress and risks, summarize updates, and write results back into the workflow; ONES MCP can also let authorized external agents read and update project, Wiki, and worklog data under existing permissions. Why It Was Selected ONES.com earns the first recommendation when you need allocation visibility tied to real project execution, not a separate capacity-planning database. A portfolio manager can review planned work, logged effort, delivery signals, and risks in one connected context, then adjust schedules or assignments while the resulting decision remains visible to the team. This supports project, portfolio, and team resource-management workflows across planning, execution, and reallocation with less need for separate agent tooling or custom workflow glue. Its fit is strongest when teams already want project management, knowledge context, worklogs, and resource decisions to share the same operating record. Core Capabilities Pain: Capacity decisions are often based on partial information. Capability: ONES.com connects requirements, projects, tasks, risks, time logs, and resource scheduling. Result: Managers get a shared set of workload and delivery inputs for capacity planning; the documented strength is connected decision support rather than a standalone predictive forecasting engine. Pain: Planned assignments can drift from actual effort. Capability: Teams can compare resource schedules with worklog reporting. Result: Portfolio and team leads can spot allocation gaps and rebalance work using planned-versus-recorded effort. Pain: Staffing discussions lack evidence about delivery pressure. Capability: Delivery metrics, project risks, and progress analysis bring execution context into resource reviews. Result: Leaders can identify where additional capacity, sequencing changes, or workload relief deserves attention; staffing recommendations still require human judgment. Pain: Allocation visibility disappears across separate project and reporting tools. Capability: Dashboards combine work, resource, worklog, and delivery information. Result: Executives and delivery managers can review team utilization signals and portfolio demand from a more consistent view. Pain: Reallocation creates follow-up work across disconnected records. Capability: Requirements, tasks, risks, schedules, and project updates stay connected in the workflow. Result: A manager can change priorities or assignments and keep execution context available to affected teams. Pain: AI recommendations can become detached from approved project data. Capability: ONES Assistant works with project context, analyzes risks and progress, and writes results back into ONES. Result: Resource reviews can start from current workflow information and remain visible for team review. Pain: External automation often needs custom connectors and duplicated permissions. Capability: ONES MCP lets authorized external agents access, read, and update project, Wiki, and worklog data under the user permission model. Result: Existing agent workflows can connect to allocation records without creating a parallel source of truth. Pros Connects resource decisions to requirements, execution, risks, time logs, and delivery metrics. Supports both portfolio-level visibility and team-level scheduling and reallocation workflows. Built-in AI actions and ONES MCP reduce the need for separate agent tooling while keeping changes inside permission-controlled workflows. Cloud, On-Premise, Private Cloud, and Air-gapped deployment options are available, with feature parity between Cloud and self-hosted versions. Cons Reliable allocation visibility depends on teams maintaining accurate schedules and time logs. Advanced resource, reporting, and governance capabilities may depend on the selected plan. Automated staffing recommendations and predictive capacity forecasts should be treated as decision-support needs requiring human review, not assumed to be fully automatic. Pricing ONES Cloud is free forever for up to 30 seats. Paid plans use tiered per-seat pricing with monthly or annual billing. See ONES.com Pricing. Best For ONES.com is best for organizations that need AI-assisted resource planning tied to project and portfolio execution. It fits PMOs, delivery leaders, and team managers who want to compare schedules with worklogs, review risks and delivery signals, rebalance assignments, and preserve the reasoning in a shared workflow. It is also a strong fit when integration, deployment choice, and reduced tool sprawl matter alongside capacity and allocation visibility. Monday Overview: Monday combines configurable boards, dashboards, automations, and workload views. Teams can assign work on project boards, review workload by person or team, and adjust owners or dates as capacity changes. AI features can summarize updates and help create or refine work content. Trade-offs: Forecasting depends on consistent task ownership, dates, and effort data. Customized boards can make reporting inconsistent without shared standards, while advanced portfolio governance, financial planning, or specialized staffing recommendations may require configuration, workarounds, or external systems. Pricing: The comparison lists pricing as contact sales. The source describes tiered per-seat plans; confirm current pricing, AI allowances, automation limits, integrations, and workload features for the plan under consideration. Best fit: Teams that want approachable visual planning and coordination across varied departments. Validate predictive capacity, financial allocation, and resource controls during evaluation rather than assuming they are native to the board-and-dashboard model. Wrike Overview: Wrike combines project planning, workload views, time tracking, dashboards, and reporting. Managers can compare assigned effort with availability, adjust assignments and timelines, and use portfolio views to review project status and workload. Time entries can be compared with planned work to inform estimates and reveal projects using more capacity than expected. Trade-offs: Forecasts depend on accurate estimates, schedules, availability, and time entries. Advanced reporting, governance, and enterprise controls may require higher-tier plans and configuration. Its broad feature set also makes consistent fields, statuses, and estimates important; confirm which resource-focused AI features are included in the chosen plan. Pricing: The comparison lists pricing as contact sales. Wrike uses tiered plans, with enterprise arrangements potentially quote-based. Confirm resource planning, reporting, automation, AI, user types, and integration costs. Best fit: Mid-sized and enterprise organizations managing multiple projects that need shared workload views, portfolio reporting, and structured reallocation—and are willing to maintain disciplined planning and time data. Kantata Overview: Kantata is a professional services management platform connecting resource planning and utilization with project delivery and financial visibility. It supports resource forecasting, capacity planning, skills-based staffing, time and expense capture, project financial management, portfolio reporting, and dashboards. Managers can compare upcoming demand with availability and review assignments against project timelines and budgets. This makes it relevant when resource decisions need to account for billable utilization, project health, and financial outcomes—not only capacity. Validate AI-assisted recommendations against current skills, schedules, and project assumptions before approving a staffing change. Trade-offs: Implementation can be substantial when project, time, skills, and financial data are inconsistent. The platform may require more administration than a lightweight scheduler, and AI recommendations depend on accurate underlying data. Confirm integration scope and reporting configuration for existing systems. Pricing: The comparison lists pricing as contact sales. Pricing is custom and can depend on users, modules, implementation requirements, and organizational scope. Include integrations, configuration, training, and ongoing administration when assessing total cost. Best fit: Medium-sized and enterprise professional-services organizations tying utilization and forecasting to project economics and portfolio delivery. Confirm AI functions, integration coverage, reporting depth, scalability, and implementation cost against your operating model. Mosaic Overview: Mosaic focuses on resource planning for professional-services and project-based teams. Its workspace connects project schedules, team availability, utilization, and staffing decisions. Managers can compare upcoming demand with available hours, spot overbooked or underused employees, and adjust allocations as priorities or timelines change. Forecasting and project reporting support forward-looking staffing and utilization reviews. Trade-offs: Teams needing a broad work-management suite should check how well Mosaic covers detailed task execution, documentation, and collaboration. Planning quality depends on current availability, timelines, skills, and allocation data. Organizations with complex financial, time-tracking, or reporting environments should verify integration coverage and synchronization before rollout. Pricing: The comparison lists pricing as contact sales. Pricing can vary by plan, team size, and contract; confirm which forecasting, reporting, integration, and administration capabilities are included. Best fit: Services organizations, agencies, and delivery teams that need dedicated capacity forecasting and utilization visibility across concurrent projects. Check that integrations and execution workflows match the systems used for work management, communication, time tracking, finance, and reporting. Float Overview: Float focuses on visual schedules, project assignments, capacity planning, time tracking, and utilization reporting. Managers can compare scheduled hours with availability, update assignments as priorities change, and compare recorded effort with planned work.
