title: PaperToProfit: Turning Handwritten Dhaba Bills into Revenue & Profit Intelligence with Open-Source AI and TabPFN
author: Sapnil M
summary: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle 🍽️ What I Built Walk into almost any local diner, roadside dhaba, tea stall, or family eatery across South Asia, and you will see the exact same analog pattern: every customer order is scribbled with a ballpoint pen on small carbon pads (Kitchen Order Tickets / KOTs) or notepad tear-offs. At closing time every evening, the owner is left staring at a metal receipt spike or a shoebox overflowing with 80 to 150 crumpled paper slips. The Problem Commercial restaurant POS systems (like Toast, Petpooja, or Lightspeed) cost anywhere from $60 to $180/month , require expensive proprietary hardware, and demand manual keypad entry during busy service. Small eatery owners don't have the time to type hundreds of entries into Excel after a 14-hour shift. Consequently, they operate in the dark: Zero Real-Time Profit Clarity: They track incoming cash, but don't know their net gross margins after food costs (COGS). Cash vs. Digital Reconciliation: They struggle to verify whether drawer cash matches digital UPI payments. Blind Menu Engineering: They cannot identify which dishes are high-margin "Stars" (like Masala Chai & Sweet Lassi) versus high-effort, low-margin "Plowhorses". Kitchen Prep Waste: Over-prepping gravies and rotis during slow hours leads to spoilage, while under-prepping during peak rush causes walkouts. The Side Hustle PaperToProfit is a mobile-first, privacy-preserving restaurant intelligence engine built specifically for neighborhood food businesses. Snap, Paste, or Upload: The cashier or owner snaps a phone photo of their slips at checkout or batches them at night. Multi-Engine Open Vision AI: Uses open-weight multimodal models (Google Gemini Flash & Groq Llama 3.2 Vision) alongside a local offline RapidOCR 2D spatial clustering engine to instantly extract messy handwritten shorthand ( "4 sp chai", "2 veg thali", "6 tandoori roti", "half chk biryani" ), quantities, and scribbled totals. 1-Tap Tactile Review: An interactive, receipt-card UI lets owners verify and adjust items with zero friction. Instant Profit & BCG Menu Matrix: Delivers real-time gross revenue, net margin estimation, hourly rush-hour heatmaps, and a 4-quadrant BCG menu engineering matrix. TabPFN Predictive Sales Intelligence: Powers next-week revenue forecasting and flags anomalous volume surges or revenue leaks using Prior Labs' TabPFN-3.5 tabular foundation model. Who would pay for this? Local tea stalls, dhabas, quick-service diners, and food-truck operators. Offering this as a managed micro-SaaS at $9 to $15/month (₹300–₹500/month) provides 10x ROI by preventing food waste and revenue leakage—with a 95%+ gross profit margin for the builder. 🎥 Demo Video Walkthrough Direct Link: Watch on YouTube (https://youtu.be/6FxF2mufxw0) Visual Walkthrough 1. Instant Bill Digitization & 1-Tap Review Screen Upload any handwritten or printed bill, snap with mobile camera, or paste directly with Ctrl + V . Items, prices, and categories are parsed with confidence scores and rendered in an editable receipt card: 2. Live Financial Dashboard & Rush Heatmap Real-time gross revenue, estimated net profit, food costs (COGS), average ticket size, 14-day revenue trajectory, Cash vs. UPI breakdown, and kitchen prep rush-hour distribution: 3. Menu Engineering BCG Matrix Automatically categorizes every dish into Stars (promote), Plowhorses (re-engineer price), Puzzles (upsell), and Dogs (drop) based on sales volume and profit margins: 4. TabPFN Predictive Sales AI & Anomaly Detection Uses Prior Labs' TabPFN-3.5 foundation model to forecast next-week revenue trajectory with confidence bounds, flag anomalous revenue spikes/drops ($|Z| > 1.6$), and provide actionable prep recommendations: 5. Scanned Bills Revenue Ledger Every verified slip is recorded in a local SQLite ledger with 1-click CSV export for taxes and accounting: Local Run: Double-click ./run.bat (or run python -m uvicorn backend.main:app --port 8000 ) to access the complete application at http://127.0.0.1:8000 . 💻 Code The complete source code is open-source under the MIT license: GitHub Repository: https://github.com/SAPNIL-M/PapertoProfit Core Architecture ├── backend/ │ ├── main.py # FastAPI REST API serving endpoints & static assets │ ├── extractor.py # Vision AI pipeline (Gemini, Groq, 2D Spatial RapidOCR) │ ├── forecaster.py # Prior Labs TabPFN-3.5 foundation forecasting engine │ ├── analytics.py # Real-time financial KPIs, rush heatmaps & BCG matrix │ ├── db.py # Zero-config embedded SQLite persistence │ └── seed.py # Realistic 14-day historical dhaba sales seeder ├── static/ │ ├── index.html # Responsive, tactile receipt UI & dashboard │ ├── app.js # Client-side reactivity, Chart.js charts, clipboard paste │ ├── style.css # Modern typography & receipt paper styling │ └── demo_slips/ # Realistic vectorized dhaba and restaurant KOTs ├── Dockerfile # Container configuration └── run.bat # 1-click Windows desktop launcher 🛠️ How I Built It PaperToProfit was engineered with a strict philosophy: zero-latency local execution, resilient multi-engine fallbacks, and zero proprietary lock-in. 1. The Vision AI & Extraction Engine Reading faded carbon copies and cursive handwriting is notoriously difficult for traditional OCR. We implemented a 3-tier cascade: Tier 1: Google Gemini Flash Vision API: Extremely capable multimodal vision model that understands culinary shorthand, abbreviations ( "2 pl dal", "4 sp chai" ), and folded edges in ~1.5 seconds. Tier 2: Groq Llama 3.2 Vision: Free cloud open-weight vision model running on ultra-fast LPUs. Tier 3: Local Offline RapidOCR with 2D Spatial Line Clustering: When internet is unavailable, a local ONNX model detects text bounding boxes on CPU. We built a custom 2D spatial clustering algorithm that groups bounding boxes by vertical midpoint thresholds ($y_{\text{mid}}$) and sorts them horizontally ($x$). This pairs dish names on the left with quantities and prices on the right, with full support for Indian currency symbols ( ₹ , Rs. , /- , INR , comma pricing). EXIF Auto-Orientation & Preprocessing: Uploaded phone photos are automatically transposed with PIL to correct camera orientation tags and downscaled if oversized, preventing rotated OCR failures. 2. Predictive Sales Intelligence with TabPFN (Prior Labs) Rather than training heavy custom time-series models (like Prophet or ARIMA) which require hundreds of data points and fail on small restaurant samples, we leveraged TabPFN-3.5 , Prior Labs' in-context tabular foundation model: Zero-Shot Tabular Predictions: Formulates time-series as tabular features ( day_of_week , day_index , recent_moving_average , order_volume ). 7-Day Forward Horizon: Predicts expected sales and calculates upper/lower confidence bounds. Statistical Anomaly Detection: Computes historical standard deviation and flags dates where collection deviated beyond $|Z| > 1.6$, providing owners with actionable operational advice (e.g., ingredient stock alerts for upcoming weekend surges). 3. Lightweight Full-Stack (FastAPI + SQLite + Vanilla JS) FastAPI: Async Python backend serving both REST endpoints and frontend assets from a single port ( 8000 ). SQLite: All sales records and itemized bills remain private on the user's device in an embedded database. Tactile UI: Built with Vanilla JS, Chart.js, and Lucide icons. Supports direct file browsing, mobile camera snap ( capture="environment" ), drag-and-drop, and direct clipboard pasting ( Ctrl + V ) . 🔓 Why Does Open Innovation Matter? For neighborhood food businesses, open-source AI isn't just an alternative—it is the only way this business model can survive: 1. The Zero-Marginal-Cost Advantage A typical neighborhood dhaba generates 100 paper slips a day (~3,000 bills/month). Using closed enterprise vision APIs (like GPT-4o or Claude 3.5 Sonnet) at $0.03 to $0.05 per image call , the raw API bill alone would cost $90 to $150 every month . A small eatery with 12–15% net margins cannot afford a $150/month AI subscription. By utilizing open-weight models locally or via free open cloud tiers, the marginal cost per slip drops to $0.00 . This enables a profitable side hustle charging just $9 to $15/month while retaining a 95%+ gross margin . 2. Complete Financial Privacy & Trust Small business owners are extremely sensitive about their daily cash drawers, tax numbers, and supplier margins. Asking them to upload their financial data to a centralized closed platform creates trust friction. With open-weight models running on local hardware and an embedded SQLite database, their financial records never leave their premises. 3. Tolerance for Regional Dialects & Culinary Slang Every region has unique handwritten slang ( "cutting chai", "1 pl paneer", "half fry", "bun maska", "2 bt naan" ). Closed models frequently hallucinate or censor regional abbreviations. Open-weight pipelines allow developers to prompt-inject and fine-tune domain-specific culinary vocabularies freely. 🤖 My Agent Session This entire project—from the FastAPI architecture and spatial line-clustering algorithm to the TabPFN predictive integration and mobile-responsive UI—was built with pair-programming assistance from Antigravity . Agent Transcript: View Agent Session Key Tasks Accelerated by Agentic Workflow: Diagnosed OCR bounding box sorting issues on multi-column receipts and designed the 2D spatial clustering algorithm. Implemented automatic EXIF transposition for mobile phone camera uploads. Integrated Prior Labs' TabPFN tabular forecasting and anomaly detection algorithms with mathematical Z-score thresholds. 👥 My First User My father is a local shopkeeper, and like millions of small shop owners and diner operators, his counter is always stacked with physical paper slips and handwritten receipts. The Test with Real Bills: To test PaperToProfit with genuine, messy handwriting rather than clean synthetic data, I pulled out an old paper slip that was lying at home from my father's collection of shop bills. Testing & Feedback: I ran the photo through the pipeline right in front of him. In less than 2 seconds, the multimodal vision engine parsed the faded ink, item names, quantities, and prices into the interactive review card, calculating the totals automatically. When he saw the app categorize the items and populate the live ledger without any manual typing, he was genuinely impressed and found it very helpful: "At the end of a long day in the shop, sitting with a pen, paper, and calculator to total up crumpled slips is exhausting. Half the time, small calculation errors slip through. Having a tool where you just point your phone camera at an old slip and it reads the numbers, saves the record, and tells you what you actually earned is a massive relief." Key takeaways & requested features: A simple one-click daily WhatsApp summary report that can be shared at closing time. Voice readout and regional language toggle to make daily ledger entries even faster. 🏆 Prize Categories Best Use of TabPFN ($200): Integrated Prior Labs' TabPFN-3.5 tabular foundation model to deliver zero-shot 7-day revenue projections and detect anomalous sales drops/surges from tabular restaurant time-series data without model training loops. 🏁 Conclusion Open-source AI has reached an inflection point where solo builders can create practical, high-impact utilities that solve real-world problems for small businesses that Silicon Valley tech leaves behind. PaperToProfit turns everyday paper trash into actionable business intelligence—private, affordable, and 100% open.

title: How we handle “the phone already knows this” — context propagation in an on-device AI agent
author: StareBrain
summary: One of the most common reactions we get from StareBrain beta users is some version of: “why do I still have to tell it things it should already know?” It’s a fair question. The phone has the calendar. It has the contacts. It has the location history, the saved addresses, the flight confirmation in the email. The information exists. The problem is that each app owns its slice of it and nothing connects the dots automatically. Building an on-device AI agent means solving that problem — not by sending everything to a cloud service, but by building a context layer that runs locally and propagates the right information to the right action at the right time. Here’s how we approached it. The problem: action context vs device context When a user says “book me a cab for my usual airport,” there are two kinds of context the agent needs: Action context : what action is being requested, what parameters it needs, what apps can fulfill it Device context : what does the phone already know that’s relevant — upcoming calendar events, saved locations, recent searches Most agent architectures handle action context well. Device context is where things get complicated, because it’s distributed across the OS and multiple apps, each with their own permission model. `data class AgentContext ( val actionIntent : ActionIntent , val deviceContext : DeviceContext , val resolvedParameters : Map < String , Any > ) data class DeviceContext ( val upcomingEvents : List < CalendarEvent >, val savedLocations : List < SavedLocation >, val recentApps : List < String >, val activeNotifications : List < NotificationSummary > ) ` The agent needs to resolve parameters from device context before dispatch — not during, and not by asking the user for information the phone already has. Context resolution before dispatch We added a resolution pass that runs before any action is dispatched. It takes the raw intent and tries to fill in missing parameters from device context before surfacing anything to the user: `class ContextResolver ( private val calendarProvider : CalendarProvider , private val locationStore : LocationStore ) { fun resolve ( intent : ActionIntent , context : DeviceContext ): ResolvedIntent { val params = intent . requiredParameters . associateWith { param -> when ( param ) { is Parameter . Location -> resolveLocation ( param , context ) is Parameter . DateTime -> resolveDateTime ( param , context ) is Parameter . Contact -> resolveContact ( param , context ) else -> UnresolvedParameter ( param ) } } return ResolvedIntent ( intent , params ) } private fun resolveLocation ( param : Parameter . Location , context : DeviceContext ): ParameterValue { // "usual airport" → check saved locations for airport category val saved = context . savedLocations . filter { it . category == param . hint } . maxByOrNull { it . useCount } return saved ?. let { ParameterValue . Resolved ( it . address ) } ?: ParameterValue . NeedsConfirmation ( param ) } } ` If a parameter can be resolved confidently, it’s filled in automatically. If it can be resolved with reasonable confidence but not certainty, it’s surfaced to the user as a pre-filled suggestion they can confirm or change. If it can’t be resolved at all, it’s flagged as missing and the user is asked. The key rule: never ask for information the phone already has. Confidence thresholds Not all resolutions are equal. “Your usual airport” from a saved location you’ve used 40 times is high confidence. “Your usual airport” inferred from one calendar event three months ago is low confidence. `enum class ResolutionConfidence { HIGH , MEDIUM , LOW , UNRESOLVABLE } data class ParameterValue ( val value : Any ?, val confidence : ResolutionConfidence , val source : ContextSource ) fun ParameterValue . shouldAutoFill (): Boolean = confidence == ResolutionConfidence . HIGH fun ParameterValue . shouldSuggest (): Boolean = confidence == ResolutionConfidence . MEDIUM fun ParameterValue . shouldAsk (): Boolean = confidence == ResolutionConfidence . LOW || confidence == ResolutionConfidence . UNRESOLVABLE ` High confidence → auto-fill, show in confirmation summary. Medium confidence → pre-fill with a “is this right?” prompt. Low confidence → ask the user directly. This keeps the agent from confidently doing the wrong thing while still reducing the number of things the user has to say. The privacy constraint Everything in this system runs on-device. No context leaves the phone. That’s a hard constraint, not a preference. The practical implication: we can’t use a cloud model to reason over the full device context, because we can’t send the full device context to a cloud model. The resolution logic has to be deterministic enough to run locally, which means it needs to be explicit about what signals it uses and how it weighs them. That’s a tighter constraint than cloud-based approaches, but it’s what makes the privacy guarantee credible. “Your data never leaves your phone” only means something if the architecture actually enforces it. What this solves (and doesn’t) Context resolution handles the “it should already know this” problem for structured data — saved locations, calendar events, contacts. It doesn’t solve open-ended inference (“what would I usually do here?”) or cross-app state that requires active reading of app content. Those are harder problems. The structured data layer is the foundation. Getting it right first means users stop being asked for things the phone already has, which is the baseline expectation before anything more ambitious makes sense. The goal isn’t to build the most capable agent. It’s to build one that never makes you feel like you’re talking to something that doesn’t know you.

title: Coding Is Easy in 2026. Getting Paid Isn’t. Here’s How to Start.
author: Robert Adamson
summary: You can build an app. You can connect a database, add authentication, integrate payments, and put it online. Then you launch. A few people visit. Someone says, “Looks cool.” Nobody pays. What comes between working code and actual income? A customer with a problem, a useful solution, and a reason to buy. If you can build software but haven’t earned from it yet, here’s a practical path to your first paying customer. Step 1: Choose how you want to earn Start by choosing one route: Route What you sell Example Freelancing A finished project Build a booking website A fixed service The same defined solution to different customers Set up appointment reminders for salons A software product Access to a tool A monthly repair shop management app If you need income soon, start by looking for a small paid project. You can sell a clear result to one customer without first building a product for hundreds of people. If you want a software business, start with one customer anyway. Their workflow will teach you what to build. Choose one route for now. You can expand later. Step 2: Pick a customer you can actually reach “Small businesses” is too broad. Choose a specific group: Independent repair shop owners. Private tutors. Local cleaning companies. Freelance photographers. Small property owners. Then ask: Can I have a conversation with five people in this group? You might find them through your existing contacts, local businesses, professional communities, or relevant online groups. Access matters. An audience you can talk to is a useful starting point. For this guide, let’s use independent repair shops. Step 3: Find an expensive or frustrating task Don’t start with: “Would you use an app I’m building?” Start with their current work: What do you repeatedly do by hand? What gets forgotten? Where do mistakes cost money? What software do you already pay for? Can you show me how you handled this last time? Imagine a shop owner tells you: “We write repair details on paper. Sometimes we forget to follow up with customers who haven’t collected their devices.” Now you have something specific to investigate. How often does it happen? How do they handle it today? Is it serious enough to change their process? Listen for real examples, not polite enthusiasm. Step 4: Turn the problem into a small offer “An all-in-one business platform” is difficult to explain and expensive to build. A smaller offer is easier to understand: “I’ll set up a repair tracker so you can see open jobs, unpaid balances, and devices waiting for collection.” Your offer should explain: Who it helps. What problem it solves. What you will deliver. What it costs. When it will be ready. For example: “I’ll build a repair tracker for your shop with ticket creation, job status, and unpaid balances. The pilot costs $150 and includes setup plus two weeks of support.” That price is an illustration, not a universal recommendation. Your price needs to reflect the work, customer value, and support involved. Step 5: Ask for a paid pilot A compliment tells you someone likes the idea. A paid agreement gives you stronger evidence that the problem matters. Ask: “Would you like to try a paid pilot with those three features?” Before taking payment, agree in writing on: What is included. The delivery date. The price and payment schedule. How changes will be handled. Support and cancellation terms. Be clear if the software hasn’t been built yet. If they decline, ask what is stopping them. It could be the price, timing, trust, or the problem itself. Use the answer to improve the offer before writing more code. Step 6: Build one complete workflow For the repair tracker, your first version might support: Create ticket → update repair status → record payment → close ticket. That workflow should work from beginning to end. You probably don’t need inventory forecasting, staff rankings, ten integrations, and a custom dashboard builder to deliver the agreed pilot. You do need the basics that make the tool dependable: correct calculations, appropriate access controls, safe handling of customer data, and a way to recover from mistakes. Keep the feature list small. Make the promised workflow reliable. Step 7: Help the first customer use it Sending a login link doesn’t mean the job is finished. Walk through a real task together. Watch where the customer pauses: Is a field confusing? Does entering a ticket take too long? Is an important detail missing? Can they find yesterday’s jobs? Fix the problems that prevent them from getting value. For a small business tool, setup and support are part of what the customer is buying. Step 8: Check whether it actually helps After they’ve used it, ask: Are you still using it? What task became easier? What do you still handle outside the tool? Would you pay to keep using it? Why—or why not? With their permission, compare the result with how they worked before. Perhaps they can now find unpaid repairs without checking a stack of paper tickets. That is a concrete benefit you can explain to another shop. Avoid inventing savings or claiming results you haven’t measured. A useful customer story is more convincing than a long feature list. Step 9: Find the next four customers Use what you learned to approach similar businesses. Your message can be simple: “I built a repair tracker that shows open jobs and unpaid balances in one place. How does your shop currently manage those?” Keep the conversation relevant and personal. Follow community rules and respect people who aren’t interested. When someone wants a demo, show their main task first. Let them see how the tool would fit their day. Track a few numbers: People you contacted. Conversations you had. Demos you gave. Customers who paid. Customers who kept using it. These numbers help you find the problem. Few replies may mean your audience or message needs work. Plenty of demos with no sales may mean the offer needs work. Step 10: Make sure the money makes sense Suppose five customers pay $20 per month. That is $100 in monthly revenue . Then subtract hosting, payment fees, any paid services, and the time you spend supporting them. Ask: “Can I serve more customers at this price without creating an unmanageable job for myself?” You may need a setup fee, a higher price, a simpler product, or a more limited support offer. Use recurring pricing when you provide ongoing value. A one-time project may fit a one-time payment better. Getting paid is the first milestone. Earning sustainably is the next. A simple plan for your first week You don’t need to finish a business in seven days. Use the week to replace guesses with evidence. Day Action 1 Choose one customer group you can reach 2–3 Have five conversations about their current work 4 Pick one repeated problem 5 Write a small offer with a price and clear scope 6 Show a sketch or demo to interested people 7 Ask for a paid pilot and learn from the response If nobody wants the pilot, investigate before building. Change the problem, customer, or offer based on what you heard. Before you start your next app Write down the answers to these questions: Who will buy it? What problem will they pay to solve? How will I reach them? What is the smallest result I can deliver well? You don’t need perfect answers. You need answers specific enough to test. Your first payment might come from a small tool for one local business. Deliver it well, understand why they bought it, and use that knowledge to find the next customer. What’s harder for you right now: finding a problem, finding customers, or asking them to pay?
